rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation while giving useful spacing information across the mixture. This should show whether peaks are unretained, held to the final hold, or spread through the gradient so later runs can trim the window and adjust slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only gain is reducing t_last below 10 min. Shorten the gradient at the same window and temperature to compress the chromatogram while checking whether the closest pair remains above R = 1.5.

The 16 min run is nearly optimal and the limiting pair is still just above baseline criterion, so take one more step shorter at the same conditions. This tests whether we can push t_last under 10 min without dropping the worst pair below R = 1.5.

At 14 min the only issue is the 6/7 pair, which looks slope-limited only modestly, so keep the fast gradient and use a 5 C temperature decrease to seek a selectivity change that may reopen that pair while staying near the 10 min target.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity badly, so probe the opposite direction at the same fast gradient. If 45 C improves the critical mid-cluster while keeping t_last under 10 min, it could beat the current best; if not, we will know 40 C is near the optimum temperature.

Since 14 min at 40 C is fastest but loses only one critical pair, try a slightly higher starting organic fraction to shift the crowded middle of the chromatogram to a different effective phi-program while keeping the last peak under 10 min. This tests whether the close pair is more sensitive to the gradient window than to temperature.

The higher phi0 improved both speed and the critical pair, so now trim the high end of the window to concentrate the gradient over the actual elution region. This may further improve the crowded mid-cluster while still keeping the last peak within 10 minutes.

The narrower upper window improved the limiting pair substantially, suggesting the critical selectivity responds to the phi-window. Trim phi1 one more step to try to push the 6/7 pair over R = 1.5 while keeping all compounds eluting before 10 minutes.

You already have a perfect CRF, so the only remaining objective is to see whether the same optimized window can be made faster without losing full resolution. Shortening tG by one step directly tests whether the current method has excess resolution margin or whether injection 8 is the true edge.

The 12 min run was too steep, so stay at 14 min and narrow the window one more step to see if the critical pair can remain fully resolved while pulling the last peak just under 10 min. This is the most plausible route to a shorter perfect method than injection 8.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical pair but stretched the last peak, so counterbalance by raising phi0 one step while keeping the successful upper bound and slope similar. This may preserve full resolution and pull t_last back below 10 minutes, potentially matching or surpassing the current best robustly.

Injection 11 achieved a perfect score with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes, so use that margin to raise phi0 one more step and test whether the run can be compressed further while retaining full resolution. This is a direct edge search around the current optimum window.

Injection 11 is perfect and raising phi0 too far hurt the critical pair, so hold phi0 at 0.15 and lower phi1 one step to see whether added selectivity in the crowded region can be kept while reducing the run edge. This explores the neighboring perfect-method space most likely to preserve R for the 6/7 pair.

We now know the sweet spot is near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, with 0.15/0.85 already perfect; checking phi1 one step higher at the same phi0 maps the other side of that local optimum. This tests whether 0.15/0.85 is the narrow best point or whether there is equal headroom on the high-phi side.

Since several neighboring windows around 0.15/0.85 are near-perfect, test a slightly shallower gradient at the best window to see whether extra resolution margin on the 6/7 pair is gained with only a modest time penalty. This helps confirm whether 14 min is truly the shortest perfect method or just the edge of a broader optimum.

With the window optimized, the only untested local lever is temperature at the best composition; a small increase could reduce t_last further while possibly preserving the now-adequate 6/7 separation. This probes whether a temperature shift can yield another perfect method with more speed margin than injection 11.

Temperature changes strongly affect the critical pair, so test whether the slower selectivity at 35 C can compensate for a steeper 12 min gradient and produce a faster fully resolved run. This directly checks a possible tradeoff between temperature and slope that has not yet been mapped at the best window.

The 12 min run at 35 C shifted the problematic pair from 6/7 to 5/6, indicating strong temperature-driven selectivity changes in the central cluster. A larger drop to 25 C at the same fast gradient tests whether that selectivity swing can separate all mid-cluster peaks enough to recover a fully resolved sub-9-minute method.

The 12 min temperature series shows strong nonmonotonic selectivity changes, so 30 C is the key missing point between the poor 25 C and 35 C runs. This is the best remaining chance to find a faster-than-14 min method that regains full resolution at the already optimized window.

The fast 12 min method fails at 25–45 C in different ways, so 50 C is the remaining nearby temperature that could move the mid-cluster into a more favorable order while keeping the run short. This closes the main unexplored temperature branch around the best composition before spending the last injections elsewhere.

The remaining unexplored local strategy is to raise both phi0 and phi1 together, keeping a 0.60-wide window but moving it laterally to match the actual elution band. This may preserve the improved 6/7 selectivity seen with narrower windows while shortening retention enough to challenge the current perfect methods.

The shifted 0.20–0.80 window also gives a perfect score, so move it one more step upward to test whether the chromatogram can be compressed further while keeping the critical pair above 1.5. This is a focused edge search around the new perfect local optimum.

Now that 0.20–0.80 at 14 min is confirmed perfect, test the corresponding 12 min version to see whether this shifted window tolerates a steeper slope better than the earlier 0.10–0.85 or 0.15–0.85 methods. It is the most promising remaining route to a shorter fully resolved method.

At 0.20–0.80 and 14 min the method is perfect with the critical pair just above threshold, so lowering phi1 one step is the best remaining way to test whether that pair gains enough selectivity to support an even tighter window. This also checks whether the late peak can stay under 10 minutes with a more focused gradient.

The 0.20–0.75 window greatly improved the limiting pair at 14 min but slightly exceeded 10 minutes, making it the strongest candidate for a successful 12 min compression. This final run tests whether that extra selectivity margin is enough to preserve full resolution while bringing the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.
